newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak opera star quits to protest state meddling.
newsitem.headline: Slovak opera star quits to protest state meddling.

text.p: International opera star Peter Dvorsky has quit the Slovak National Theatre in protest against what he calls government meddling in the arts, the theatre's director said on Thursday.
Dvorsky, a Slovak tenor, linked his decision to resign after 24 years with the recent sacking of National Theatre director Dusan Jamrich by Culture Minister Ivan Hudec.
"I have left because I don't agree with this cultural policy ...I am afraid I cannot accept this any more," the independent daily Pravda quoted Dvorsky as telling the Bratislava-based Radio Twist.

The man who replaced Jamrich, Miroslav Fischer, confirmed that he had received Dvorsky's resignation letter on Wednesday but said he wanted to meet the star tenor. "I would like us to discuss all the circumstances surrounding his departure," Fischer told the state news agency TASR.
Dvorsky has a villa in Bratislava but performs extensively abroad including recently at the Vienna State Opera.

Slovak artists have been outspoken in their criticism of the government which they say is increasingly authoritarian. The acting profession is the latest group with which the government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar has locked horns.
Earlier this month, National Theatre actors went briefly on strike to protest against Jamrich's removal and other state moves which they say constitute meddling in the arts.

Meciar is also at odds with President Michal Kovac, the opposition, the independent media, leaders of Slovakia's Hungarian minority, the medical profession and from time to time his coalition partners.

Hudec accused Dvorsky of siding with Kovac, a bitter enemy of Meciar. "I have noted he ... has begun to participate in all the activities held by the president, or people linked with the political opposition in Slovakia," he said in a statement.
Dvorsky said he would not return to the National Theatre unless action was taken over Jamrich.
"They (government officials) would have to apologise to him and then advertise a normal competition for both the posts of director and general manager of the opera," he said.
An estimated 10,000 people demonstrated recently over the government's arts policy and at least 35,000 have signed a petition protesting demanding that Hudec resign.
Actors suspended their stoppage after three days but remained on a strike alert.
Ladislav Snopko, a former culture minister and Meciar critic expressed dismay. "The crisis in culture is the most serious since the World War Two," he said on Thursday.

But Meciar's stand is uncompromising. "We have more state-sponsored theatres than other nations...All of them choose any drama they wish, any art direction and cast they want, they show what they want," he told a recent rally.
Playing on nationalist dislike of the neighbouring Czech Republic, he said: "If they want to kiss arses in Prague, let them do it, but don't let them consider this Slovak culture."
